prompt: I'm reading the AArch64 Lightweight Fault Isolation (LFI) target. Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. Why each of these?
key: From llvm/docs/LFI.md (added with the AArch64 LFI target in #167061 on 2025-12-16). The rewrites ('expansions') run at the very end of the pipeline, in the assembler step, so that they also apply to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly, not only to compiler-generated code. The x30 guard (add x30, x27, w30, uxtw) is deferred to the next control-flow instruction so a signed return address stays intact and a following authentication instruction such as autiasp can run before the guard, which would otherwise destroy the pointer-authentication (PAC) signature. The sandbox is 4GiB and 4GiB-aligned because every guard forms the address from the sandbox base in x27 plus the low 32 bits of the register, zero-extended ([x27, wM, uxtw] / add x28, x27, wM, uxtw); with an aligned base, a full 64-bit pointer that is already in the sandbox maps to itself. The ABI keeps pointers as full 64-bit values rather than 32-bit offsets from the base, which enables stores-only mode (loads not sandboxed, stores are) and lets the host pass pointers directly into the sandbox.

sources.quote: These rewrites (also called "expansions") are applied at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step). This allows the rewrites to be applied to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly.

Deferral keeps a signed return address intact so that a following authentication instruction (such as `autiasp`) can run before the guard, which would otherwise destroy the pointer authentication signature.

This is because LFI's ABI stores pointers as their full 64-bit values, rather than just 32-bit offsets from the base. This enables stores-only mode, where loads are not sandboxed but stores are, and allows the host to directly pass pointers to the sandbox.
Memory accesses are rewritten to use the `[x27, wM, uxtw]` addressing mode if it is available, which is automatically safe.
